description: We are the top dogs. We love replit, but we love Nasa more.
summary:
ARES Maps is an interactive Mars map that enables you to explore the planet and plan your journey using actual NASA imagery and science data. You pick your point of origin, your destination and your mode of transport (walking, rover or cargo rover). In the Jezero terrain area for instance it will work out the slopes and then compare the various routes on the basis of distance, climbing and historical dust storm data. It will give you an estimated time of travel in sols and Earth days, hours and minutes. You can also look at the globe, view the real rover panoramas and check the Mars clock.

Our project is about bringing the information from a number of different missions into one map. It's designed to help students appreciate why the shortest route may not necessarily be the easiest and to illustrate the impact of terrain and the environment on exploration. Any routes that lie outside the area of detailed terrain are clearly marked as illustrative and historical observations are clearly differentiated from the current situation.
details:
We've developed ARES Maps, a web app that makes Mars a lot easier to explore and understand. It comes up as a globe and you can either search for a named location or click on a point on the map. You then pick a start point and a destination and select your mode of transport (walking, rover or cargo rover) to work out a journey. The app will then show you the route, the distance and the estimated travel time in sols and in Earth days/hours/minutes.

Within our detailed Jezero terrain coverage the app uses ground heights derived from USGS via NASA CTX stereo imagery to calculate slopes and then to search for a route using distance, uphill effort and historical dust storm data. Each transport mode has different assumed speeds and slope limits which allows the model to opt for a longer route around a slope if the climb would be more expensive. These are our project assumptions rather than the actual vehicle specifications. Outside of the terrain coverage the routes are purely illustrative as we can't derive any reliable slopes from the surface imagery alone.

The map is a combination of NASA surface imagery, colour imagery, elevation shading and day/night infrared mosaics. Mars View allows you to look around actual rover panoramas. Other features include a Mars clock, estimated daylight, stops and an estimated travel range. There's also historical radiation measurements, local soil chemistry and a dated Curiosity weather report to give some context. It's important to note that this does not provide a live safety forecast or a full chemical hazard map.

We built the app using HTML, CSS and JavaScript (Leaflet for the flat map and Three.js for the globe). It's hosted on GitHub Pages so you can just open it via a link in a browser. Python was used for the data prep, the research calculations and the document generation. OpenAI Codex was our go-to for debugging the code and Google NotebookLM was used to generate the narration for our 30 second demo over the slides, as well as for the 3-5 second video explainer.

Our idea is to present the complex mission data in terms of familiar map controls. We've thought about data coverage, transport differences, travel times, uncertainty and how to explain the layers to someone who doesn't have any space background. The primary objective is to enable the non-specialist to explore the NASA data and to understand the decisions that go into planning a journey to Mars.
